stepTexts.stir_fry_veg: Add carrot, cabbage, shiitake and kamaboko and toss another 2–3 minutes. Keep the vegetables bright and slightly crisp because they continue cooking in the soup.
stepTexts.simmer_soup: Pour in the prepared soup and bring to a lively simmer. Add bean sprouts and cook about 2 minutes, skimming any foam; the broth should be savoury and full-bodied but not milky.
stepTexts.add_noodles: Add champon noodles directly to the wok and simmer 3–4 minutes, or according to the package, so they absorb the soup. Return the seafood to perfect doneness, divide noodles and toppings between bowls and serve immediately.

recipe_000043.title: Classic Miso Soup with Tofu and Wakame
recipe_000043.description: A simple everyday Japanese soup where dashi provides umami and miso is dissolved at the end for a fragrant, rounded finish. Tofu and wakame make the classic combination, but the salt level should always be adjusted to the specific miso used.
recipe_000043.animeContext: Inspired by the traditional home-food atmosphere of Demon Slayer. This is a culinary-cultural association rather than a claim about one exact bowl shown in a particular episode.

miso.name: White, awase or red miso paste

stepTexts.rehydrate_wakame: Soak dried wakame in cool or lukewarm water for about 5 minutes until expanded. Drain well and squeeze gently; a small amount grows significantly, so do not over-portion it.
stepTexts.heat_dashi: Bring dashi to a gentle simmer. Taste it plain before seasoning so you know how salty your miso needs to be; different miso brands vary considerably in salt level.
stepTexts.warm_tofu: Lower the heat and add tofu cut into 1–1.5 cm cubes. Warm for about 2 minutes without vigorous boiling, which can break the delicate tofu.
stepTexts.dissolve_miso: Turn off the heat. Put miso in a ladle or fine strainer, loosen it with hot dashi and dissolve it back into the pot. Start with less, taste, then add more if needed; avoiding a hard boil preserves the freshest miso aroma and flavour.
stepTexts.finish: Add drained wakame and sliced scallion. Reheat only gently if necessary, without bringing the soup to a rolling boil, and serve immediately.

recipe_000044.title: Japanese Caramel Purin
recipe_000044.description: A smooth Japanese caramel custard with a firm but trembling set and a glossy bitter-sweet sauce released when unmoulded. Gentle mixing and low-temperature bain-marie cooking prevent bubbles and keep the texture almost glassy.
recipe_000044.animeContext: Inspired by Gintama’s well-known affection for sweets and parfait-style desserts. This purin card is an editorial sweet-tooth association, not an episode-specific claim.

stepTexts.make_caramel: Put caramel sugar and cold water in a small light-coloured saucepan. Heat without stirring until the syrup turns deep amber, swirling the pan gently. Remove from heat and carefully add the hot water away from your face; it will spit. Divide immediately among four ramekins.
stepTexts.warm_milk: Warm milk with custard sugar and vanilla until steaming but not boiling, stirring to dissolve the sugar. Remove from the heat and let it stand a minute so it is hot but not violently scalding.
stepTexts.mix_eggs: Whisk whole eggs and yolk gently just until uniform. Avoid incorporating air: bubbles create holes instead of the smooth, dense texture characteristic of purin.
stepTexts.temper_filter: Pour warm milk slowly into the eggs while stirring continuously. Strain the custard through a fine sieve twice, then skim visible foam. Divide over the set caramel and cover the ramekins loosely with foil.
stepTexts.bain_marie: Place ramekins in a deep tray and add hot water to halfway up their sides. Bake at 150°C for 25–30 minutes. The edges should be set while the centre still gives a gentle unified wobble rather than sloshing.
stepTexts.cool_chill: Remove from the water bath, cool until no longer hot, then refrigerate at least 3 hours. Full chilling lets the custard finish setting and the caramel loosen into a sauce.
stepTexts.unmould: Run a thin knife around the edge, place a plate over the ramekin and invert decisively. If it resists, hold the base in warm water for a few seconds, dry it and try again.

recipe_000045.title: Ebi Fry — Panko-Fried Shrimp
recipe_000045.description: Straight, crisp Japanese fried shrimp with a coarse panko shell and juicy interior. Small cuts release the abdominal tendons so the shrimp fries almost straight, while careful tail drying reduces oil splatter.
recipe_000045.animeContext: Inspired by the school-and-family food atmosphere of My Hero Academia. No exact ebi-fry scene is claimed without direct evidence.

stepTexts.clean_shrimp: Remove the heads and peel the shrimp, leaving the last shell segment and tail attached. Make a shallow cut along the back and remove the dark intestinal vein, then rinse quickly and pat dry.
stepTexts.straighten: Make 3–4 shallow diagonal cuts across the belly without slicing through. Turn the shrimp over and gently press along the back until the muscle fibres relax and the shrimp lies almost straight; do not crush the flesh.
stepTexts.dry_season: Trim the sharp tail tip and scrape or squeeze out trapped water from the tail fins to reduce dangerous splattering. Pat every shrimp very dry, then season lightly with salt and pepper.
stepTexts.bread: Set up flour, beaten egg and panko in separate trays. Coat each shrimp in a thin layer of flour, then egg, then panko, pressing crumbs onto the body while keeping the tail free.
stepTexts.fry: Heat oil to 175–180°C. Fry only 3–4 shrimp at a time so the oil quickly recovers its temperature; cook about 2–3 minutes, turning once, until the panko is deep golden and the shrimp opaque and firm.
stepTexts.drain_serve: Drain upright or on a wire rack so steam escapes from the crust. Serve immediately with shredded cabbage, lemon and tartar sauce or Japanese mayonnaise.

recipe_000046.title: Isobeyaki (Isobe-maki) Mochi
recipe_000046.description: Grilled kirimochi brushed with soy sauce and wrapped in crisp nori, a simple Japanese snack built entirely on texture and umami. It is commonly called Isobeyaki and is also described as Isobe-maki; the mochi should be blistered outside and molten-chewy inside.
recipe_000046.animeContext: Inspired by K-On!’s tea-time snack culture. The culinary preparation is real, but the app does not claim a specific Isobeyaki scene without direct evidence.

stepTexts.make_sauce: Stir soy sauce with the optional sugar until dissolved. A plain soy version is also traditional; use sweetness only if you like the glossy sweet-savoury style.
stepTexts.toast_first_side: Place kirimochi in a dry non-stick pan over medium-low heat and cover. Toast about 5 minutes, checking occasionally, until the lower face is golden and the centre begins to puff.
stepTexts.toast_second_side: Turn the mochi and cook uncovered for about 3 minutes more, until the second face is lightly blistered and the centre is fully soft and stretchy. Remove as soon as it puffs strongly so it does not burst and leak.
stepTexts.coat: While the mochi is piping hot, brush or dip both faces in the soy mixture. Return to the pan for only 20–30 seconds per side if you want the sauce lightly caramelized; watch closely because soy and sugar burn quickly.
stepTexts.wrap_serve: Wrap each mochi immediately with a strip of crisp nori and serve hot. The contrast is best at once: as cooked mochi cools it firms and loses the soft elastic texture.

recipe_000047.title: Sanshoku Soboro Don
recipe_000047.description: A classic tricolour Japanese rice bowl of sweet-savoury ground chicken, tiny soft egg curds and a bright green vegetable stripe. The defining technique is continuous stirring so both chicken and egg become fine, even soboro rather than large pieces.
recipe_000047.animeContext: Inspired by Food Wars!’ focus on technique and presentation. The dish itself is a real Japanese home-cooking and bento staple; the anime connection here is editorial rather than an episode claim.

stepTexts.season_chicken_cold: Put ground chicken, ginger, soy sauce, mirin, sake and sugar in a cold saucepan. Break the meat apart thoroughly before turning on the heat; starting cold makes it easier to create the very fine, even crumbs characteristic of soboro.
stepTexts.cook_chicken: Set over medium-low heat and stir constantly with several chopsticks or a whisk-like motion, scraping the bottom and breaking every clump. Cook 6–8 minutes until the chicken is fully cooked, finely crumbled and the liquid has reduced to a moist glaze rather than a puddle.
stepTexts.mix_eggs: Beat eggs with sugar and salt only until homogeneous. Use a clean small saucepan so the yellow colour stays bright.
stepTexts.cook_egg_soboro: Cook eggs over low to medium-low heat, stirring rapidly and continuously with chopsticks. Break up curds as soon as they form and remove from heat while they are still moist, before they become dry rubbery crumbs.
stepTexts.prep_green: Blanch or reheat the peas just until bright green and hot, then drain very well. If using another green vegetable, cut it into small neat pieces so the three-colour pattern remains distinct.
stepTexts.assemble: Divide steaming rice between two bowls. Cover one third with chicken soboro, one third with fine egg soboro and place a narrow green stripe between them. Serve hot, or cool promptly and safely if packing for bento.

recipe_000048.title: Chawanmushi — Savoury Steamed Egg Custard
recipe_000048.description: A delicate Japanese steamed egg custard suspended in dashi with small pieces of chicken, shrimp, mushroom and fish cake. The signature texture is almost silken: a balanced egg-to-dashi ratio, straining and very gentle steam prevent holes and curdling.
recipe_000048.animeContext: Inspired by the careful home-cooking focus of Today's Menu for the Emiya Family. No exact chawanmushi episode is claimed without direct scene evidence.

stepTexts.prep_fillings: Cut chicken and shiitake into small pieces. Quickly blanch or sear the chicken until the exterior is no longer raw, and briefly blanch the shrimp if they are thick; the gentle custard steam should finish, not rescue, large cold raw fillings.
stepTexts.mix_seasoned_dashi: Season lukewarm dashi with usukuchi, mirin and a small pinch of salt. Let it cool to lukewarm or room temperature; hot stock can begin setting the egg before the mixture is strained.
stepTexts.mix_eggs: Break the eggs and stir gently with chopsticks or a whisk without beating air into them. Measure roughly 100 ml egg for two large eggs and use about 250 ml dashi for the classic soft set.
stepTexts.strain_fill: Combine egg and seasoned dashi slowly, then pass through a fine sieve. Divide chicken, shrimp, shiitake and kamaboko between two heatproof cups and pour in the custard to about three-quarters full; pop or skim surface bubbles.
stepTexts.steam: Cover the cups. Steam over high heat for about 2 minutes to heat them, then reduce to very gentle steam for 10–12 minutes. The water should not violently boil around the cups or the custard will turn porous.
stepTexts.check_finish: The surface should be smooth and set while the centre gives a delicate wobble. Insert a thin skewer: clear broth should appear around it, not raw egg. Garnish with mitsuba and serve warm.

recipe_000049.title: Kashiwa Mochi
recipe_000049.description: A Children’s Day wagashi of soft rice cake filled with smooth anko and wrapped in a fragrant kashiwa oak leaf. The leaf is a ceremonial, aromatic wrapper rather than food; using prepared culinary leaves and the correct joshinko flour is essential.
recipe_000049.animeContext: Inspired by Ranma ½’s broad connection to traditional Japanese sweets and comic food scenes. No exact kashiwa-mochi appearance is claimed without direct episode evidence.

stepTexts.prep_leaves_filling: Use only kashiwa leaves sold for culinary wrapping, not leaves gathered outdoors. Rinse prepared or salt-pickled leaves and drain; if your package specifies boiling/soaking, follow it. Divide anko into eight smooth 25 g balls.
stepTexts.mix_dough: Whisk joshinko and sugar together, then add most of the water gradually until the mixture is thick but smooth and ribbon-like. Hold back a little water because different rice flours absorb differently.
stepTexts.cook_mochi: Cover loosely and microwave in short stages, stirring between them, until the dough is fully cooked, opaque-white to slightly translucent and very hot, about 3–4 minutes total depending on microwave power. Follow package guidance if your joshinko behaves differently.
stepTexts.knead: Transfer to a heatproof surface or bowl and knead with a wet spatula, then with damp hands once cool enough, until the dough becomes smoother, shinier and pliable. Do not over-knead until tough.
stepTexts.shape_fill: Divide into eight equal pieces. With damp hands shape each into an oval, flatten it, place one anko ball slightly off-centre and fold into a half-moon, sealing the edges gently without thinning them to tears.
stepTexts.wrap_serve: Wrap each filled mochi in one prepared kashiwa leaf with the decorative side outward. The leaf perfumes and protects the sweet but is not eaten. Serve at room temperature, preferably the same day.

recipe_000050.title: Gintama-style Giant Japanese Fruit Parfait
recipe_000050.description: A towering Japanese kissaten-style parfait layered with ice cream, whipped cream, fruit and crunchy cereal, pushed into an intentionally extravagant anime presentation. Japanese fruit parfait is a real café dessert; the giant scale here is the app’s playful Gintama-inspired variation.
recipe_000050.animeContext: Parfait is a verified recurring Gintama motif around Gintoki’s sweet tooth. A direct platform reference is season 3 episode 40 (overall episode 139), where Gintoki is treated to parfait; the oversized composition here remains an original app interpretation.

stepTexts.chill_glasses: Chill two tall sturdy parfait glasses for at least 5 minutes. A cold glass slows melting and buys time while you build the upper layers.
stepTexts.whip_cream: Whip the cold cream to firm but smooth peaks and transfer to a piping bag. Stop before it becomes grainy; the cream needs enough structure to support fruit and wafers.
stepTexts.prep_fruit: Wash and dry the berries thoroughly. Slice strawberries and banana immediately before assembly and keep a few attractive pieces whole for the top; wet fruit makes the layers slide.
stepTexts.build_base: Add a thin ribbon of sauce to each glass, then a layer of cornflakes or granola. Add a small amount of whipped cream and press a few fruit slices against the glass for visible colour.
stepTexts.layer: Add vanilla and matcha ice cream, alternating with more fruit and whipped cream. Work quickly and keep the ice cream scoops separated by solid ingredients so the structure does not collapse.
stepTexts.finish_serve: Pipe a tall final swirl of cream and decorate with Pocky, wafer, reserved fruit and a cherry. This deliberately oversized anime-style version should be served immediately with a long spoon before the ice cream melts into the crunchy layers.

recipe_000051.title: Shio Ramen
recipe_000051.description: A practical bowl of Shio Ramen, built around well-cooked noodles, a balanced broth or sauce and toppings added at the right moment so texture stays distinct.
recipe_000051.animeContext: This recipe is thematically inspired by Emiya-san Chi no Kyou no Gohan, Naruto. The association is kept as inspiration only; no specific episode or on-screen appearance is claimed without direct evidence.

sale_marino_fine.name: Sea salt fine (o alga kelp salata)

stepTexts.step_1: Prepare the broth or seasoning base first and keep the toppings organized, so every component is ready before the noodles are cooked.
stepTexts.step_2: Cook the noodles separately until just tender, then drain very thoroughly; avoid leaving them in hot water because they will continue to soften.
stepTexts.step_3: Finish the broth or sauce at a gentle simmer and combine the hot components only when their seasoning and texture are balanced.
stepTexts.step_4: Assemble the noodles immediately, add the prepared toppings in distinct sections and serve while the broth, noodles and garnishes still contrast clearly.

recipe_000052.title: Kare Pan
recipe_000052.description: A crisp Kare Pan with a dry, well-set coating and a juicy or creamy center, cooked in controlled oil and served before the crust softens.
recipe_000052.animeContext: This recipe is thematically inspired by Black Butler (Kuroshitsuji), My Hero Academia. The association is kept as inspiration only; no specific episode or on-screen appearance is claimed without direct evidence.

curry_giapponese_denso_ben_freddo.name: Curry giapponese denso ben freddo (preparato con potatoes, carrots e ground meat)

stepTexts.step_1: Prepare the filling or main ingredient, season it evenly and dry or chill it as needed so the coating can adhere without slipping.
stepTexts.step_2: Coat or batter the pieces in the stated order, keeping the outer layer light and even rather than pressing it into a dense shell.
stepTexts.step_3: Fry in small batches at controlled temperature until the exterior is deeply crisp and the center is fully cooked or heated through.
